readingInstruction: Read Joshua 13:1-17:18. This is a long reading in the geographic style of the book, and it can feel like a list. Don’t try to memorize the places. Read it for the shape: the land is being divided among the tribes, and God is distributing an inheritance. Keep your eye out for Caleb in chapter 14 and the daughters of Zelophehad in chapter 17.
settingTheScene: The conquest is over, at least in principle, but there is still much land to be taken. Joshua is old, and God tells him to divide the territory among the tribes so that each can finish the work. The next several chapters read like a land registry. For many modern readers they are the most skippable part of the Bible. But for the first readers, they were among the most precious. This was proof that God had kept his promise to Abraham: he had given his people a place. Each border and town was a statement that this family belongs here. For us, the lists point toward a greater inheritance.
observation: God tells Joshua, “You are old and advanced in years, and there remains yet very much land to possess” (13:1).
Moses had already given the eastern territory to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh (13:8-33).
“To the tribe of Levi alone Moses gave no inheritance. The LORD God of Israel is their inheritance” (13:33).
Caleb, at eighty-five, asks for the hill country of Hebron and says, “Give me this hill country of which the LORD spoke on that day” (14:6-12).
Hebron becomes Caleb’s inheritance “because he wholly followed the LORD” (14:14).
Judah’s allotment is the longest and is described first (15:1-63), though Judah could not drive out the Jebusites in Jerusalem (15:63).
Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons of Joseph, receive the central hill country, and Ephraim does not drive out the Canaanites in Gezer (16:10).
The daughters of Zelophehad ask for and receive an inheritance among their father’s brothers (17:3-6).
interpretation:
The land lists are not an interruption of the story but its fulfillment. From Genesis 12, God had promised Abraham a land. Four hundred years of waiting, a slavery in Egypt, and forty years in the wilderness had passed. Now, tribe by tribe and family by family, the promise is distributed. God keeps his word down to the details of boundary lines. The lists are the opposite of vague spirituality. They show that God’s promises have addresses.

Several details shine out. First, the Levites receive no territory because “the LORD God of Israel is their inheritance.” This is one of the great lines of the Old Testament. They have cities to live in, but their portion is God himself. It is a picture of what is true for every believer. Whatever else we may have or lack, our true inheritance is the Lord. Psalm 16, which you will read soon, will express the same idea: “The LORD is my chosen portion.”

Second, Caleb’s request is a remarkable story of long-term faithfulness. He is eighty-five years old, and he asks for the hardest land in the region, a hill country full of giants. He does not ask for retirement. Forty-five years earlier, he and Joshua had stood against the report of the other spies. He says, “I wholly followed the LORD my God.” His strength is the same at eighty-five as at forty, and he is ready for the fight. The text marks him out as a model of perseverance. His faith did not fade with age. It deepened.

Third, the daughters of Zelophehad ask for what they are due. God had already promised in Numbers 27 that daughters could inherit when there were no sons, and now they remind Joshua. The story shows God’s care for the vulnerable and the importance of claiming what has been promised.

But there are also shadows. Judah cannot drive out the Jebusites. Ephraim does not drive out the Canaanites at Gezer. These small notes of incomplete obedience foreshadow the book of Judges. The land is given, but Israel must take it. Many of God’s gifts work this way: the inheritance is secure, but we must live into it. Paul says the same about our salvation, “work out your own salvation… for it is God who works in you” (Philippians 2:12-13).
connection: The land promise is rooted in Genesis 12:7, 15:18-21, and 17:8. The Levites’ inheritance appears in Numbers 18:20 and Deuteronomy 10:9. Caleb’s story begins in Numbers 13-14. The daughters of Zelophehad first appear in Numbers 27 and 36. The “inheritance” language runs into the New Testament in Ephesians 1:11-14, Colossians 1:12, and 1 Peter 1:3-4, where believers have an imperishable inheritance kept in heaven.
application:
First, consider your inheritance. If you are in Christ, you have been given the Spirit as a guarantee of an inheritance that cannot fade. Let that anchor your view of what you do and do not have this week.

Second, learn from Caleb. Where might you be tempted to coast in your faith? Ask the Lord for the kind of faith that still asks for the hill country at eighty-five.

Third, notice that Israel’s incomplete obedience begins in small places. Is there a “Gezer” in your life, an area of compromise you have chosen not to confront? Name it and ask for help.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for keeping his promises down to the last detail.
Ask for a wholehearted faith like Caleb’s.
Ask him to show you where you have left territory unclaimed.
